finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id has no effective authorization. authorize() is called without await, so its 403 rejection is discarded and the report is deleted for any caller, including one without a delete grant or an anonymous one.
finding.source: Any HTTP DELETE /reports/:id. Precondition: caller lacks a 'delete' grant on the report, or req.user is undefined.
finding.sink: db.reports.remove(report.id) at server.js:21, followed by 204 at server.js:22.

trace.note: req.user = req.session.user; anonymous or unprivileged callers yield undefined or a non-granted user.
DELETE handler entered with attacker-chosen req.params.id.
report = await db.reports.get(id).
authorize(req.user,'delete',report) is not awaited; its returned promise is discarded.
Inside authorize, if grants lack 'delete', line 14 throws 403. Because authorize is async, this becomes a rejected promise that the handler never observes.
Handler continues immediately and deletes the report.
Responds 204.

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is authorize() at server.js:9-16, and it is not awaited at line 20. No auth middleware, try/catch, or error handler exists in this file. The PUT route at line 27 does await, so the bypass is specific to DELETE.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only guard is authorize() at server.js:9-16, and its result is never checked: line 20 is a bare call with no await, so its rejection (thrown at line 14, or a TypeError at line 10 if req.user is undefined) is an unobserved promise. Line 21 runs regardless. No auth middleware, try/catch, or error handler appears in server.js. The PUT route at line 27 awaits authorize, so the bypass is specific to DELETE.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so the 403 rejection from server.js:14 never stops execution, and server.js:21 deletes the report and server.js:22 returns 204 for any caller, including an anonymous one (req.user undefined from server.js:5). The file shows no other control; the attacker needs only network access to the endpoint, with no privilege required.

finding.claim: Denied, anonymous, or not-found requests produce unhandled promise rejections, which can crash the Node process (remote DoS). DELETE is affected under any Express version. PUT is affected under Express 4, which does not catch rejected async handlers.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated or unprivileged request to DELETE or PUT /reports/:id, or any request for a nonexistent id. Precondition: Node 15+ default unhandled-rejection behavior.
finding.sink: Unhandled rejection from authorize() at server.js:20 (DELETE), or from the awaited authorize() at server.js:27 (PUT) propagating out of the async handler.

trace.note: req.user may be undefined for anonymous callers.
report may be null for a nonexistent id.
db.grants(user.id, resource.id) throws TypeError if user or report is null. Inside async authorize, this becomes a rejection.
DELETE: the rejection is unhandled because the promise is not awaited, which can crash the process.
PUT: await rethrows the 403 or TypeError into the handler. Express 4 does not catch it, so it becomes an unhandled rejection.

finding.guards_checked: No try/catch, no .catch on the promise, no process.on('unhandledRejection') handler, and no error middleware in this file. Whether the crash occurs depends on the Express version and Node version, which are not in this directory.

verdict.guard_found: none. server.js has no auth middleware or error handler. The only middleware (server.js:4-7) just copies req.session.user to req.user, and authorize() (server.js:9-16) has no try/catch. The DELETE call at server.js:20 is a bare, un-awaited statement, so its rejection is unhandled. The only process-level handler is absent (no process.on('unhandledRejection') anywhere in the file).
verdict.reason: An anonymous or low-privilege request to DELETE /reports/:id reaches authorize() at server.js:20 with req.user undefined (server.js:5) or a null report (server.js:19). This throws inside the async function at server.js:10 or the 403 at server.js:14, and the rejection is never awaited or caught, so Node 15+ crashes the process. The PUT claim (server.js:27) depends on the Express version, which is not in this directory, so that half is UNVERIFIABLE on its own, but the DELETE half is confirmed.

finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT. The entire request body is passed to the update, so a caller with 'write' on a report can set any column the database allows, such as owner, id, or access fields.
finding.source: req.body of PUT /reports/:id (attacker-controlled JSON). Precondition: caller holds a 'write' grant on the report.

trace.note: express.json() parses the body into req.body with no field allow-list.
Authorization checks only the 'write' action on the report, not which fields are being changed.
req.body is passed directly to db.reports.update.

finding.guards_checked: Only the grant check at line 27. There is no field allow-list, no schema validation, and no removal of id, owner, or ACL fields. The schema of db.reports is not in this directory, so the exact impact is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)` checks only the action on the report. It returns nothing, so the check gates the call but not the fields. No allow-list or schema validation exists between server.js:3 `express.json()` and server.js:28 `db.reports.update(report.id, req.body)`. Nothing removes id, owner, or ACL keys from the body.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: express.json() at server.js:3 populates req.body, the awaited write check at server.js:27 gates only the action, and server.js:28 passes the whole body to db.reports.update, so any field the caller sends reaches the update. The attacker must already hold a 'write' grant (server.js:10-15), which does not normally include changing ownership or ACLs, so this is a real escalation path. The specific impact on owner, id, or access columns is unverified because db.reports' schema is not in this directory.

finding.claim: No authentication enforcement and no session middleware in this file. req.session is read unguarded, so every request throws a TypeError (500) if no session middleware is mounted, and req.user is undefined for anonymous callers. The authorization layer then depends entirely on F1 and F2 being fixed.
finding.source: Any HTTP request. Precondition: session middleware is absent or does not populate session.user.
finding.sink: req.session.user at server.js:5, and req.user consumed by authorize() at lines 20 and 27.

trace.note: Global middleware runs on every request.
Dereferences req.session without a null check.
authorize dereferences user.id with no null check.

finding.guards_checked: No session or auth middleware is visible in this file. The file may be a fragment of a larger app, so this is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none. server.js:3 is only express.json(), and the global middleware at server.js:4-7 dereferences req.session with no null check. The directory contains only server.js, so no session or auth middleware is mounted anywhere in scope. authorize() (server.js:9-16) dereferences user.id at line 10 with no guard, so an undefined user throws there.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: server.js:5 reads req.session.user unguarded, so with no session middleware (none exists in this directory) every request hits a TypeError and returns 500, and server.js:10 throws for an anonymous req.user. Impact is limited to crashes and fail-closed 500s on PUT; the authorization bypass comes from the un-awaited authorize() at server.js:20, which is F1's territory, not F4's.

finding.claim: req.params.id is passed unvalidated to db.reports.get and db.reports.remove/update. If the db layer builds queries by string concatenation, this is an injection sink. The db module is not present, so this is an unverified candidate.
finding.source: req.params.id in DELETE or PUT /reports/:id (URL path, attacker-controlled).

trace.note: id taken directly from the URL path with no type or format check.
Same for PUT.

finding.guards_checked: None in this file. The db implementation is not visible, so exploitability cannot be confirmed.

verdict.guard_found: None in server.js. server.js:19 and :26 pass req.params.id straight to db.reports.get with no type or format check. The db module is not in the directory (Glob returned only server.js), so whether the value is parameterized, allowlisted, or concatenated into a query cannot be determined.
verdict.reason: Both trace lines match the claim (server.js:19 and :26 pass req.params.id unvalidated to db.reports.get), but the injection sink lives in the missing db module, and the attacker's role is not set by any visible auth middleware (server.js:5 only copies req.session.user), so exploitability cannot be decided from server.js alone. Separately, server.js:20 calls authorize without await, so the DELETE handler's authorization check does not gate the removal at server.js:21; that is a distinct authorization bug that the F5 claim does not cover.
